summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Colombian courts have also intervened directly in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The source inventory establishes no department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding for Arauca. What is documented for this department is the national pattern of lethal violence against trans people, episodic state response and armed-group activity elsewhere in the country, with no Arauca-specific aggravation or protection on the record.

Nationally the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025; 41 trans women were killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. The assault was filmed and the video went viral from 5 April 2025; she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one was arrested. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was".

Armed groups continue to threaten trans people in territories under their control. In Caquetá, "social cleansing" flyers appeared on streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men gave the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The armed-group threat pattern documented elsewhere in Colombia has no sourced counterpart in Arauca, but it sets the ceiling for what a trans visitor could face in departments where armed groups operate. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyers threatened a further wave of "social cleansing" targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", and trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work; a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Economic marginalisation compounds the risk: discrimination limits trans women in Colombia mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which concentrates exposure to the men who threaten them.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Other fatal attacks recalled in the sources include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.
